piece.dm_text:
Here is how voice AI agents work for MSME order calls:
1. Model Selection: Gemini 3.8 Live handles simple voice calls at lower cost per turn. Gemini 3.8 Extended Thinking handles complex multi-step reasoning and price negotiations, though it costs more per token.
2. Guardrail Control: Set exact rules before triggering calls (e.g., in Google's demo, setting a price floor of Rs 400 per item).
3. Call Answering: Startups like Equal AI deploy voice assistants to handle incoming calls before you pick up.
4. Language: Gemini Live supports over 25 Indian languages and dialects.

[80] YourStory — From multi-lingual AI agents to the future of voice: Google Cloud’s Naren Kachroo at TechSparks 2026
URL: https://yourstory.com/2026/11/from-multi-lingual-ai-agents-to-the-future-of-voice-google-clouds-naren-kachroo-at-techsparks-2026
From multi-lingual AI agents to the future of voice: Google Cloud’s Naren Kachroo at TechSparks 2026 | YourStory Sidebar is Loading... ADVERTISEMENT For Naren Kachroo, the most useful AI is the kind that finishes the job. “There is no value created without the task actually getting completed with AI,” said Kachroo, Head of Sales & GTM AI at Google Cloud. At TechSparks 2026, during a product showcase titled ‘Voice AI in action’, Kachroo walked through Google’s latest voice models, customer use cases, and a live demo built for small businesses. His argument was: voice is becoming the main way people will interact with AI, and in India, that shift will happen in local languages and accents.
Kachroo said the industry has moved past treating generative AI as a question-and-answer tool. “We have moved from thinking about generative AI as chatbots, as something that we ask questions of and we get answers from,” he said.
The focus now is AI that has access to tools, data, and capabilities, and can take actions on a person’s behalf.
“We are not building AI for the sake of AI,” he added. The goal, he said, is AI that improves how people live and work everyday.
Google recently announced Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking . Gemini 3.8 Live can detect and switch between 97 supported languages within the same conversation. Kachroo explained how businesses should choose between the two models.
Gemini 3.8 Live suits simpler conversational and agentic tasks, such as a live voice chat with basic tool calling. Extended Thinking suits conversations that need deeper reasoning, context switching, and multiple steps. Cost also matters, he noted: Extended Thinking costs more per token.
Both are voice-to-voice models, which handle speech as input and output in a single model. For developers who need only one part of that pipeline, Google also offers separate models for text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and live translation.
Kachroo said the latest Gemini text-to-speech model performed strongly in Google’s internal testing with Indian languages, accents, and tonality.
Kachroo played a series of short demos to show the range of use cases.
In the first, Shopify’s assistant, Sidekick, guided a merchant step by step through connecting a domain in the Shopify admin. In the second, a voice agent booked a restaurant table for eight people. Midway, the caller asked whether a cake was allowed, shared a photo from Google reviews to ask whether a dish was vegetarian, and asked about other vegetarian options before confirming.
The second demo required the agent to track context across multiple turns, remember preferences, and make several tool calls. That kind of task, Kachroo said, is where Extended Thinking fits.
He also showed Live Avatar, which pairs Gemini’s live voice with real-time video generation and lip-syncing, so users see an animated face as well as hear a voice. Google made Live Avatar available to businesses through Gemini Enterprise recently, and marks the audio and video it generates with an invisible SynthID watermark. Citi was a pilot customer: its Citi Sky assistant, built with Google DeepMind’s real-time avatar technology and the Gemini Live API, walks US wealth clients through options, such as what to do with a maturing certificate of deposit.
Kachroo said Gemini 3.8 Live has the lowest cost per turn of any comparable model, and that Extended Thinking tops industry benchmarks for speech-to-speech quality.
Google has said Extended Thinking scored 82.6 on Artificial Analysis’ speech-to-speech quality index, the highest overall score.
The low price is not a land grab, he said. Google runs the full stack itself, from its TPU chips and infrastructure to the models and applications, and passes the efficiency gains on to customers. That lets Google offer both a top-quality model and a lower-cost workhorse model.
He pointed to two customers as examples of voice AI in use: Autotrader, which uses the technology for buying and selling used cars, and Equal AI, an Indian startup whose assistant answers and handles phone calls before the user picks up.
The centerpiece of the session was a live demo of an assistant for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which Kachroo said his team built in about a day. It is a large potential market: more than 7.8 crore enterprises were registered on the government’s Udyam portal as of February 2026, according to the MSME ministry. Kachroo flagged one risk upfront: he was running it on a mobile hotspot after failing to connect to the hotel network.
The demo featured a fictional safety gear company and its owner, Rajesh, who had just received about 500 helmets. Speaking to the assistant, Rajesh asked how many leads he had for helmets. The assistant found two: a construction firm in Mumbai that needed 500 helmets, and a hardware store in Agra that needed 50.
Rajesh told the assistant to drop the smaller lead, send a quotation to the Mumbai buyer, and call them to close the deal. He set one condition: the price had to stay above Rs 400 per helmet, and the assistant could book the order without coming back for approval.
The assistant then called the buyer and negotiated in Hindi. Kachroo said it carried context from the internal conversation with Rajesh into the external call, negotiated on the company’s behalf, and closed the deal.
That end-to-end flow is where Google wants voice AI to go, he said. With the 3.8 Live models, he believes businesses can now build voice agents into their processes that complete tasks on their own.
Kachroo said the assistant could have held the same conversation in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Marathi, and other languages. That matters, he argued, because the Indian consumer is moving voice-first. Gemini Live itself now supports more than 25 Indian languages and dialects . According to the IAMAI-Kantar Internet in India 2024 report, 98% of India’s 886 million active internet users accessed content in Indic languages, and one in five used voice commands to go online.
“I believe that voice is the future,” he said. Voice AI in India, he added, will need to be native to the languages people speak, the accents they use, and what they are most comfortable with.
Kachroo said Google DeepMind has a team in Bengaluru researching voice, focused on Indian accents and cultural nuances. Google also funds Project Vaani, run by the Indian Institute of Science and ARTPARK, which has open-sourced more than 31,000 hours of speech in 105 languages from 165 districts.
Kachroo closed with an invitation for founders and developers to try the models, use the experiences, and share feedback, including what does not work, so that Google’s research and product teams can improve them. His larger point was that voice AI is ready to move beyond conversation into execution, and that India, with its range of languages and its voice-first users, is one of the markets where that shift will be tested first.

[84] YourStory — Gemini in action: How voice, agents, and coding tools are changing the way businesses use AI
URL: https://yourstory.com/2026/11/gemini-in-action-how-voice-agents-and-coding-tools-are-changing-the-way-businesses-use-ai
Sidebar is Loading... ADVERTISEMENT Gemini in action: How voice, agents, and coding tools are changing the way businesses use AI | YourStory Generative AI, in the form most people know it, is only about three years old. In that short time, Rajesh Shewani believes it has already moved through three distinct eras.
First came retrieval: chatbots that answer a question and wait for the next one. Then came agents that take action on a user’s behalf. Now, he said, the industry is entering what he calls the harness era, where orchestration, memory, and guardrails around a model let it carry out work from start to finish.
“An agent is nothing now but a model plus a harness,” said Shewani, Head of AI Customer Engineering for Digital Natives, Startups and ITeS at Google Cloud, at TechSparks 2026 .
In a masterclass titled ‘Gemini in action’ , Shewani promised a look at what is happening rather than a sales pitch. He covered where businesses are putting AI to work, how voice is becoming an interface, the tools Google uses to build its own software, and the questions organisations need to answer as agents become everyday users of their systems.
Shewani said organizations are no longer just discussing AI but executing in five broad areas.
Agents, which are changing how companies work and how startups build for other businesses.
Creative work, from image and video generation to marketing and branding, was one of the earliest areas to take off.
Multimodal AI, which lets models work with images, video, and voice, not just text.
Physical AI, including robotics and self-driving cars, which he expects to grow fast as the “brain” of large language models gains a body.
AI fluency, a priority for traditional organizations in banking, insurance, retail, and telecom.
For those traditional businesses, the worry is less about building models and more about whether employees can use AI in their daily jobs. They don’t need to be experts or developers, he said, but they do need to be fluent.
The three eras are cumulative, Shewani explained. Agents build on retrieval, and harnesses build on agents. AI is no longer an assistant that appears and disappears, but something closer to an autonomous colleague.
“It’s no longer just about the model,” he said. “It’s the model plus everything that you build around it”, from memory and context management to sandboxing.
He described four things every agent needs:
A goal: booking a ticket, making an entry in an SAP system, or negotiating a price by voice.
Instructions: guidance that goes beyond a single prompt and can be stored for reuse, much as new employees learn how an organization works.
Knowledge: a company’s own data, since models are trained on public information, not internal records.
Tools: the means to act, such as updating a CRM or placing an outbound call.
Knowledge is where much of the effort is going. Many teams had begun building their own “LLM wikis” for agents, and Google is now trying to standardize the approach with the Open Knowledge Format (OKF). OKF v0.1 represents knowledge as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, which agents can read directly. Shewani compared its role to what Model Context Protocol (MCP) did for backend integration.
A shared knowledge layer, combining a knowledge graph with plain text, also keeps costs down, he said. Rather than querying everything for every prompt, agents are pointed to structured context, which uses fewer tokens.
“Voice is becoming the new user interface,” Shewani said, whether for customers, employees, or users who prefer to speak in local languages. He noted that Google DeepMind’s team in Bengaluru is doing extensive work on Indic languages. Gemini Live now supports more than 90 Indian languages and dialects , including Sanskrit, Bhojpuri, and Maithili.
He showed a live translation demo built for Grab, the Southeast Asian ride-hailing platform, in which a passenger and driver who do not share a language coordinate a pickup.
Grab says travellers and driver-partners make more than 10 million voice calls a month, and it has been testing Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, which offers two-way translation in more than 70 languages.
Shewani said Gemini 3.8 Live, launched in September, improves further on noise cancellation and conversations between multiple speakers.
Another demo, built in India, dubbed a news video into Marathi and Malayalam from a single prompt while matching lip movements and facial expressions. Dubbing once required complex pipelines with many steps, he said, but live models have cut those down significantly, making it easier to create training videos and marketing content across languages.
He also showed Citi Sky, Citi’s AI-powered wealth assistant, which uses a virtual avatar to walk clients through options for a maturing certificate of deposit and complete the renewal. For such experiences, latency is critical. “If a flow breaks even for a second or a millisecond, it doesn’t work,” he said.
Shewani then walked through the tools that sit beneath these experiences.
Gemini agent is a single agent that can carry out tasks end to end. Google Cloud introduced it on October 8, 2026, and it can keep working in the cloud for hours or days, even when a user’s device is offline.
Shewani gave the example of a procurement team asking it to research options, write a request for proposal, send it to vendors, evaluate responses, and produce a shortlist. According to Google, the agent routes each task to the most suitable model, currently choosing between Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude models.
Gemini Enterprise adds guardrails and quotas for businesses, which Shewani said helps keep costs from running away, a key concern in tokenomics. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian has said nearly 90% of Fortune 100 companies use Gemini Enterprise.
Antigravity is Google’s harness for building software, available as a command-line tool and as extensions for code editors. Shewani said most of Google’s own code is now written using the same harness, known internally as Jetski. Google CEO Sundar Pichai has said 75% of new code at Google is now generated by AI and reviewed by engineers, up from 25% in October 2024.
CodeMender scans code for vulnerabilities, creates patches, tests them in a sandbox, and can integrate with a GitHub repository. When Google DeepMind first announced it in October 2025, it had already contributed 72 security fixes to open-source projects.
Google is also giving every agent its own identity, which Shewani likened to an LDAP directory for agents, so organisations can track which agent took which action.
No model can be cheapest, fastest, and most capable at once, Shewani said, so businesses need a range of models and should match each task to the right one. Google’s Flash models are its workhorses for everyday tasks that do not need complex reasoning.
“If I need to get to office every day, I don’t need to have a Ferrari,” he said. For the hardest work, there is Gemini 4 Argon.
